Statistics question bank — teacher review packet

1647 items to review (all new items plus 9 corrected baseline items). Numeric items were independently recomputed; items marked conceptual need a hand check of the key and distractors. Flags: key-longest = the correct option is the longest (guessing cue); similar-to = near-duplicate of another item in the same cell; implied-input = a number is implied by wording rather than printed. Mark each item Approve, Revise, or Remove. The same list is in review-sheet.csv for spreadsheets.

Anticipating Patterns

Probability: Long-Run Relative Frequency and the Law of Large Numbers — CP2

stat-u3-s01-cp2-x01 · multiple-choice · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
A weather forecast says there is a 30% chance of rain tomorrow. What does this mean?
  • It will rain in 30% of the area for sure.
  • It will rain for 30% of the day.
  • It will not rain, because 30% is less than 50%.
  • ✓ On many days with conditions like tomorrow's, it rains on about 30% of them.
Answer: On many days with conditions like tomorrow's, it rains on about 30% of them.
Solution: Probability is a long-run relative frequency over many similar situations.
Flags: conceptual; key-longest

Probability: Long-Run Relative Frequency and the Law of Large Numbers — CP1

stat-u3-s01-cp1-x01 · multiple-choice · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
A coin is tossed 10 times and lands heads 7 times; later it is tossed 1,000 times and lands heads 512 times. Which statement is best supported?
  • The proportion of heads should be exactly 0.5 after 1,000 tosses.
  • ✓ The 1,000-toss proportion (0.512) is a much better estimate of P(heads) than the 10-toss proportion (0.7).
  • The coin is biased toward heads because 0.7 > 0.5.
  • The 10-toss result is more reliable because it is more recent.
Answer: The 1,000-toss proportion (0.512) is a much better estimate of P(heads) than the 10-toss proportion (0.7).
Solution: The law of large numbers: relative frequency settles near the true probability as trials increase.
Flags: conceptual; key-longest

Solution: Independent trials have no memory; past results do not change future probabilities.

Probability: Long-Run Relative Frequency and the Law of Large Numbers — HONORS

stat-u3-s01-honors-x01 · multiple-choice · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
After 1,000 tosses of a fair coin, there are 520 heads. As tossing continues to 100,000, what most likely happens?
  • Tails must catch up so the counts become equal.
  • The proportion of heads will move further from 0.5.
  • The proportion stays at 0.52.
  • ✓ The proportion of heads gets closer to 0.5, even though the difference between the number of heads and tails may not shrink.
Answer: The proportion of heads gets closer to 0.5, even though the difference between the number of heads and tails may not shrink.
Solution: LLN works by swamping, not compensating: the proportion converges while the count difference can grow.
Flags: conceptual; key-longest

Addition and Multiplication Rules — CP2

stat-u3-s02-cp2-x01 · multiple-choice · Practice · numeric, independently recomputed
At a school, 45% of students play a sport, 30% are in a club, and 12% do both. Find P(sport or club).
  • 0.14
  • 0.75
  • ✓ 0.63
  • 0.12
Answer: 0.63
Solution: General addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). / = 0.45 + 0.3 − 0.12 = 0.63.
☐ Approve   ☐ Revise   ☐ Remove   Notes: ______________________________
stat-u3-s02-cp2-x02 · multiple-choice · Practice · numeric, independently recomputed
A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is P(heart or king)? Round to four decimal places.
  • 0.2500
  • 0.3269
  • ✓ 0.3077
  • 0.0769
Answer: 0.3077
Solution: P(heart) = 13/52, P(king) = 4/52, P(king of hearts) = 1/52. / P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 ≈ 0.3077.

  • (a) Find and interpret E(X). → E(X) = 1.95; over many weekdays the dealership averages about 1.95 cars sold per day
  • (b) Find σ_X. → σ_X = √1.2475 ≈ 1.117
  • (c) A salesperson earns $100 per day plus $500 per car sold. Find the mean and SD of daily earnings E = 100 + 500X. → Mean $1,075; SD = 500(1.117) ≈ $558.5
  • (d) Find the mean and SD of total vehicles T = X + Y. What assumption did you use? → Mean 2.95; SD = √(1.2475 + 1) ≈ 1.499, assuming X and Y are independent
Answer: E(X) = 1.95; σ_X ≈ 1.117; earnings mean $1,075, SD ≈ $558.5; total mean 2.95, SD ≈ 1.499.
Solution: E(X) = 1.95. / E(X²) = 5.05, so Var(X) = 5.05 − 1.95² = 1.2475 and σ_X ≈ 1.117. / Earnings: μ = $1,075, σ ≈ $558.5. / Total: μ = 2.95, σ = √2.2475 ≈ 1.499. / Rubric (1 point each): / (a) E(X) = 0(0.10) + 1(0.25) + 2(0.35) + 3(0.20) + 4(0.10) = 1.95; over many weekdays the dealership sells about 1.95 cars per day on average. / (b) Var(X) = Σ(x − 1.95)²P(x) = 1.2475, so σ_X ≈ 1.117. / (c) Mean = 100 + 500(1.95) = $1,075; SD = 500(1.117) ≈ $558.5 (adding $100 does not change the SD). / (d) Mean = 1.95 + 1.0 = 2.95; SD = √(1.2475 + 1²) ≈ 1.499, which requires X and Y to be independent (variances add).
Flags: corrected; conceptual

stat-u3-s06-honors-x02 · short-answer · Error Analysis · numeric, independently recomputed
Error analysis. X has mean 50 and SD 6. A student finds the SD of Y = 10 − 2X as follows: “σ_Y = 10 − 2(6) = −2.” Identify the error and give the correct mean and SD of Y.
Answer: SD is unaffected by adding 10 and is multiplied by |−2|: σ_Y = 12; μ_Y = 10 − 2(50) = −90.
Solution: Adding a constant shifts the mean but not the spread. / Multiplying by −2 multiplies the SD by |−2| = 2. / σ_Y = 2 × 6 = 12 (an SD cannot be negative). / μ_Y = 10 − 2(50) = −90.

Quartiles, Percentiles, Box Plots, and Comparing Distributions — HONORS

stat-u1-t1-046 · open-response · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
KenKen completion times (seconds) for two classes: Period 2: 38, 41, 44, 45, 47, 49, 50, 52, 53, 55, 58, 62 Period 5: 35, 39, 40, 42, 43, 44, 46, 48, 51, 57, 71, 96
  • (a) Find both five-number summaries and use a common, labeled scale for parallel boxplots. → Period 2: 38, 44.5, 49.5, 54, 62; Period 5: 35, 41, 45, 54, 96 (common scale about 30–100 seconds)
  • (b) Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to identify and plot any outliers. → Period 2 fences 30.25 and 68.25: no outliers. Period 5 fences 21.5 and 73.5: 96 is an outlier and is plotted separately
  • (c) Compare shape, center, spread, and outliers in context. → Period 2 is roughly symmetric; Period 5 is skewed right with a high outlier. Period 5 has a lower median (45 vs 49.5 s) and a larger IQR (13 vs 9.5 s)
  • (d) Which class was typically faster? Justify using an appropriate statistic. → Period 5, because its median time (45 s) is lower; the median is appropriate because Period 5 is skewed with an outlier
Answer: P2: 38, 44.5, 49.5, 54, 62 (no outliers). P5: 35, 41, 45, 54, 96; fences 21.5 and 73.5, so 96 is an outlier.
Solution: Period 2: Q1 = median(38…49) = 44.5, M = 49.5, Q3 = median(50…62) = 54, IQR = 9.5, fences 30.25 and 68.25 → no outliers. / Period 5: Q1 = 41, M = 45, Q3 = 54, IQR = 13, fences 21.5 and 73.5 → 96 is an outlier. / P5 is skewed right with a typically faster (smaller) time; P2 is more consistent in the middle 50%. / Rubric (1 point each): / (a) Correct five-number summaries for both classes and a common, labeled scale. / (a) Identifies 96 as the only outlier (P5 fences 21.5 and 73.5; P2 fences 30.25 and 68.25) and plots it separately. / (b) Compares shape (P2 roughly symmetric; P5 skewed right), center (medians 49.5 vs 45), spread (IQR 9.5 vs 13) and the outlier, in context. / (c) Chooses Period 5 as faster based on the smaller median (45 s vs 49.5 s) and explains that the median is used because of the skew/outlier.
Flags: corrected; conceptual

stat-u2-t1-019 · open-response · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
A large university wants to estimate the mean amount of money students spent on textbooks this semester using a sample of 500 students. The university has 22,000 students in four class years.
  • (a) Describe how to select an SRS of 500 students. → Number the students 1–22,000 and use a random number generator to select 500 different numbers (ignore repeats); survey those students
  • (b) Describe a stratified random sample of 500 students using class year. → Separate the students by class year and take an SRS from each year (for example 125 per year, or proportional to class size)
  • (c) Explain why stratifying by class year could improve the estimate. → Spending is likely similar within a class year but different between years, so stratifying reduces the variability of the estimate
  • (d) Describe a source of bias in using the first 500 email responses and its possible effect. → Voluntary response/nonresponse bias: early responders may differ (e.g., more engaged students who buy more books), so the mean could be overestimated
Answer: (a) SRS by labels and random numbers; (b) SRS within each class year; (c) less variability because strata are internally similar; (d) voluntary response bias with a stated direction
Solution: (a) Label 1–22,000; randomly generate 500 unique integers. (b) Strata = class year; SRS in each stratum; homogeneous within strata. (c) Voluntary/first-responder bias; responders may differ systematically from all students. / Rubric (1 point each): / (a) Numbers all 22,000 students 1–22,000, uses a random number generator (or table) to choose 500 different labels, ignoring repeats; or an equivalent slip method. / (b) Separates students by class year and takes an SRS from each (e.g., 125 each or proportional allocation). / (b) Explains that textbook spending is likely similar within a class year but differs across years (e.g., upperclassmen in specialized courses), so stratifying reduces variability. / (c) Names voluntary response/nonresponse bias and gives a direction in context (e.g., students who check email often or feel strongly respond first, which may over- or underestimate spending) with justification.

Solution: (a) Voluntary response bias; people with strong opinions (likely skateboarders or strong opponents) respond, so results may be distorted toward extreme views / (b) Convenience sample/undercoverage; park users likely support a new park, so support would be overestimated / (c) Nonresponse; follow up with nonresponders by phone or a second mailing (or undercoverage of residents without a listed address) / (d) Plan 3, because random selection from a list of the population avoids self-selection and convenience bias / Scoring guide (4 points): / 1 point each part; direction of bias required in (a) and (b).

Observational Studies and Experiments — HONORS

stat-u2-s04-honors-x01 · multiple-choice · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
A study of 100,000 adults finds that those who use a standing desk have lower rates of back pain. Which additional evidence would most strengthen a causal claim?
  • A larger observational study of 1,000,000 adults
  • A higher correlation in the same observational data
  • ✓ A randomized experiment assigning adults to standing or sitting desks showing the same difference
  • Testimonials from standing-desk users
Answer: A randomized experiment assigning adults to standing or sitting desks showing the same difference
Solution: Only random assignment removes confounding from self-selection; more observational data cannot.

  • Testing whether a cough syrup reduces coughing

  • Comparing two teaching methods in randomly assigned classes
Answer: Studying whether living near a highway is associated with childhood asthma
Solution: You cannot ethically or practically assign children to live near highways; the others can be experiments.

  • ✓ Other variables besides income (such as diet, exercise, or health awareness) may still differ between the groups.
  • Income cannot be a confounding variable.
  • Organic food has no effect.
  • Controlling for one variable removes all confounding.
Answer: Other variables besides income (such as diet, exercise, or health awareness) may still differ between the groups.
Solution: Statistical adjustment handles only the variables measured; unmeasured lurking variables can remain.

A news article states: “A study of 3,500 middle schoolers found that those who play competitive sports have 15% higher test scores. Parents should sign their kids up for sports to boost grades.”
  • (a) Was this study likely an observational study or an experiment? Explain. → Observational; students (or families) chose whether to play sports
  • (b) Identify a lurking variable and explain how it could produce the association. → Family income or parental involvement: it can make both sports participation and higher scores more likely
  • (c) Is the article's recommendation justified? Explain. → No; an association from an observational study does not show that sports cause higher scores
  • (d) Describe an experiment that could test whether sports participation causes higher scores, and one practical obstacle. → Randomly assign willing students to a sports program or a control activity for a semester and compare score changes; obstacle: students/families may not comply with assigned activities
Answer: (a) Observational; students (or families) chose whether to play sports; (b) Family income or parental involvement: it can make both sports participation and higher scores more likely; (c) No; an association from an observational study does not show that sports cause higher scores; (d) Randomly assign willing students to a sports program or a control activity for a semester and compare score changes; obstacle: students/families may not comply with assigned activities
Solution: (a) Observational; students (or families) chose whether to play sports / (b) Family income or parental involvement: it can make both sports participation and higher scores more likely / (c) No; an association from an observational study does not show that sports cause higher scores / (d) Randomly assign willing students to a sports program or a control activity for a semester and compare score changes; obstacle: students/families may not comply with assigned activities / Scoring guide (4 points): / 1 point each part; (d) requires random assignment and a comparison.

stat-u2-s04-honors-x05 · short-answer · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
Explain the difference between an explanatory variable and a confounding variable, using this example: an observational study finds that cities with more police officers have more crimes.
Answer: Explanatory variable: number of police officers. A confounding variable such as city population is related to both police numbers and crime counts, so its effect cannot be separated from that of police.
Solution: The explanatory variable is the one we think may explain the response (police officers). / Population size affects both the number of officers and the number of crimes. / Because population changes with police numbers, its effect is mixed (confounded) with any effect of police. / Comparing crime rates per resident would reduce this problem.

stat-u2-t2-023 · open-response · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
Researchers want to compare a new shampoo formula with the old formula. They have 50 volunteers: 30 women and 20 men. Researchers believe hair type differs by gender.

  • (b) Describe a randomized block design using gender. → Block by gender: randomly assign 15 women to each formula and 10 men to each formula; compare formulas within each block
  • (c) Explain why blocking may improve the comparison here. → Gender is expected to affect the response, so comparing within blocks removes that variability and makes a formula difference easier to detect
  • (d) Explain what can and cannot be concluded without random selection. → Random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion about the formulas, but without random selection the results apply only to volunteers like these
Answer: (a) completely randomized 25/25; (b) block by gender, randomize within; (c) blocking reduces variability due to gender; (d) causal conclusion for similar volunteers only
Solution: Completely randomized: 25/25 random split. / Block: by gender, randomize within. / Causal conclusions are justified for subjects like the volunteers only. / Rubric (1 point each): / (a) Randomly assigns 25 volunteers to each formula (e.g., slips/numbers), applies treatments, and compares a clearly stated response (hair rating). / (b) Blocks by gender and randomly assigns formulas within each block (15/15 women, 10/10 men); compares within blocks. / (b) Explains that blocking removes variability due to gender, making differences between formulas easier to detect. / (c) Can infer that the formula causes a difference (random assignment) but cannot generalize beyond volunteers like these (no random selection).

Statistical Inference

Confidence Intervals: Point Estimates, Standard Error, and Margin of Error — CP2

stat-u4-s01-cp2-x01 · short-answer · Practice · numeric, independently recomputed
In a random sample of 400 teens, 132 said they read for fun weekly. Find the point estimate p̂ and its standard error (four decimals).
Answer: p̂ = 0.3300, SE ≈ 0.0235
Solution: p̂ = 132/400 = 0.3300. / SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) = √(0.3300·0.6700/400) ≈ 0.0235.

Answer: p̂ = 0.3800, SE ≈ 0.0396
Solution: p̂ = 57/150 = 0.3800. / SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) = √(0.3800·0.6200/150) ≈ 0.0396.

A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (42.6, 48.2). What are the point estimate and the margin of error?

  • Point estimate 45.4; margin of error 5.6
  • Point estimate 42.6; margin of error 48.2
Answer: Point estimate 45.4; margin of error 2.8
Solution: Point estimate = midpoint = (42.6 + 48.2)/2 = 45.4. / Margin of error = half the width = (48.2 − 42.6)/2 = 2.8.

A coin is flipped 100 times and lands heads 62 times. Test H₀: p = 0.5 vs Hₐ: p > 0.5. Find the test statistic (two decimals) and P-value (four decimals), then state the decision at α = 0.05.
Answer: z ≈ 2.40, P-value ≈ 0.0082; reject H₀
Solution: p̂ = 62/100 = 0.6200. / z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n) = (0.6200 − 0.5)/√(0.5·0.5/100) ≈ 2.400. / P-value ≈ 0.0082. / Since P < 0.05, reject H₀.

stat-u4-t2-023 · open-response · Practice · conceptual (review by hand)
Better Batteries: a company claims its new battery lasts more than 29 hours on average. An SRS of 15 batteries had lifetimes (hours): 27.4, 28.1, 28.9, 29.3, 29.6, 29.9, 30.2, 30.4, 30.8, 31, 31.1, 31.5, 31.9, 32.3, 33.
  • (a) State the hypotheses, parameter, and significance level. → H₀: μ = 29 vs Hₐ: μ > 29, where μ is the true mean lifetime (hours) of the new batteries; α = 0.05
  • (b) Name the test and check its conditions. → One-sample t test. Random: SRS. 10%: 15 < 10% of all batteries. Normal: n < 30 but the data show no strong skew or outliers
  • (c) Calculate the sample statistics, test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value. → x̄ ≈ 30.36 h, sₓ ≈ 1.547 h, t ≈ 3.41, df = 14, P-value ≈ 0.0021
  • (d) Conclude in context and describe a Type I error. → Because 0.0021 < 0.05, reject H₀: convincing evidence the mean lifetime exceeds 29 hours. A Type I error would be concluding the mean exceeds 29 hours when it actually does not
Answer: (a) H₀: μ = 29, Hₐ: μ > 29; (b) one-sample t, conditions met; (c) t ≈ 3.41, df 14, P ≈ 0.0021; (d) reject H₀; Type I error described

  • ✓ reject H₀ when H₀ is actually true
  • reject H₀ when it is false
  • fail to reject H₀ when H₀ is false
  • fail to reject H₀ when it is true
Answer: reject H₀ when H₀ is actually true
Solution: Type I = false alarm.

  • ✓ fail to reject H₀ when H₀ is actually false
  • accept Hₐ when it is true
  • reject H₀ when H₀ is true
Answer: fail to reject H₀ when H₀ is actually false

Regression output (n = 50): slope b = 2.1, SE_b = 0.7. If the same data were reported with x measured in units 10 times larger (so b and SE_b are each 10 times larger), what happens to the t statistic?
  • It becomes 10 times smaller.
  • It becomes 10 times larger.
  • It becomes 100 times larger.
  • ✓ It stays the same (3.0).
Answer: It stays the same (3.0).
Solution: t = b/SE_b; both scale by the same factor.
